name: First Amendment

waypoints.name: SR-20 turnout below Le Petit Cheval (east of Washington Pass)
waypoints.note: SR-20 turnout ~2 mi east of Washington Pass; climber's trail descends to cross Early Winters Creek before ascending to the formation.
waypoints.directions: Drive SR-20 to the turnout below Le Petit Cheval, roughly 2 miles east of Washington Pass. Park in the turnout itself; the climbers' trail drops from its west or southwest end, so leave the car toward that end. The turnout is the trailhead — there is no side road, and the path down toward Early Winters Creek is unmarked apart from occasional cairns.

waypoints.name: Le Petit Cheval Upper Mountain
waypoints.note: Shared upper section for Le Petit Cheval's multi-pitch routes.
waypoints.directions: Follow the cairned climbers' path down into the trees, cross Early Winters Creek on logs, and climb the rocky drainage and talus to the base of Spontaneity Arete, marked by tree snags on the left before the gully. Traverse about 250 yards across the northwest face on 3rd and 4th-class ledges to a 100 ft chimney just right of centre, then climb the route's eight technical pitches to where it joins Spontaneity Arete.

waypoints.name: Le Petit Cheval summit
waypoints.directions: Finish on Spontaneity Arete's last one and a half scrambly ridge pitches, via the Goldie Crack, to the summit.

approach_variants.name: Highway turnout east of Washington Pass, then a long ledge traverse across the face
approach_variants.notes:
Park in the highway turnout about two miles east of Washington Pass, near milepost 165, at roughly 4,900 ft. Nothing is signed.

The climbers' path drops steeply from the west end of the turnout through loose dirt and rock into the trees, marked here and there by cairns, crosses Early Winters Creek on logs, and climbs into an open rocky drainage and talus below the formation. The old line finishes with two or three informal fixed ropes across an avalanche path; a newer variation bears right just before them and needs only a little scrambling.

This route sees very few ascents, so current conditions beta effectively does not exist and there will be no traffic to follow. Budget the extra time the traverse costs on top of the walk in.
approach_variants.season: July through September, once the creek crossing and approach snow have gone
hazards: The base is a 250-yard third and fourth-class traverse away from the obvious start
Very few ascents, so no chalk, no traffic and no current conditions information
The crux comes off a belay high on the route in thin cracks with sparse protection; knifeblades and thin pins are useful
Dirty and vegetated cracks in places
Descent is by the neighbouring route's rappels or its loose gully, not by reversing this line
approach_variants.baseFinding:
You do not start where the path ends. Arrive first at the base of the formation's trade route — identified by tree snags on the left as the ground steepens, before the gully. From there, traverse about two hundred and fifty yards across the face on third and fourth-class ledges, finishing just right of centre on the north-west face. That traverse is the approach to this climb and it is the piece everyone underestimates.

The test that you have gone far enough is the first pitch itself. It is a hundred-foot chimney and hand crack ending on a large ledge, and it is easy — around 5.4. If the ground in front of you is steep or technical at the very start, you have stopped short. A hundred feet of easy chimney to a big ledge is the signature.

Confirm on the pitches above, because the low ground is not distinctive. Pitch two is a slightly vegetated hands-and-fists corner. Pitch three follows the same corner then breaks right on thin face climbing to a ledge with a cave. Pitch four is finger cracks to a large slabby ledge. Corner, then a cave ledge, then a slabby ledge: that sequence is the line.

Negative markers, and both are easy to fall into. If you racked up at the snags and started climbing without traversing, you are on the trade route — much easier, and it will feel like it. If your first pitch is protected by bolts, you are on the partly bolted four-pitch line beside the gully; this route's first pitch has no bolts, and its only fixed hardware is higher up — two bolted belays and a single bolt at the crux.

Be warned that the line is not continuously natural and some cracks are dirty and vegetated. That is the character of the route rather than evidence you are off it. The crux comes late, right off a belay high on the climb, in very thin cracks with sparse protection.

At the top it joins the trade route for its final scrambly ridge pitches, and the descent is that route's line: rappel it, or take the third-class gully on climbers' right, which is faster and loose.

permit: No climbing or wilderness permit required; Northwest Forest Pass (or day fee) to park at developed trailheads.
descent_text: The original route description does not specify a descent; because the route joins Spontaneity Arête's line for its final pitch(es), parties most likely descend via that route's rappel line (about 9 rappels with a 60m rope) or its gully descent option.
